headline: Make everyday work easier to follow.
throughline: Lead with the request handoffs and the desk guide: both show how I turn practical feedback into a change a team can use. Keep the equipment prototype available as a story about open decisions.

signals.title: Make responsibility visible.
signals.reason: The request trial separates who receives a task from who owns the next step. It shows design judgment and a shared operating routine.
signals.summary: A shared list and weekly review made the next owner clearer.

signals.title: Revise the detail that stops someone using it.
signals.reason: The guide changed after supervised use exposed an unclear escalation rule. The useful evidence is the revision and its retention for induction.
signals.summary: Supervised use exposed an unclear escalation rule in the desk guide.

stories.takeaway: I made the next owner visible, then revised the trial with the coordinators.

chapters.title: Find where requests lose their next owner
chapters.text: Requests crossed the front desk, events and facilities. I traced the routes and drafted a shared request list, aiming to clarify ownership without adding another application.

chapters.title: Test the routine with the team
chapters.text: Contributor 02 proposed a weekly review, which I facilitated. The coordinators defined the handoff rules and maintained the list. I simplified the status labels after their feedback and removed a priority field that people interpreted differently.

chapters.title: Describe the result at its actual scope
chapters.text: The coordinators continued the weekly review after the trial. We did not collect a baseline or measure turnaround. I would describe continued use, rather than claim a speed improvement.

timeline.text: Mapped the existing routes, drafted the list and facilitated the trial. Separate milestone dates were not recorded.
Revised status labels after coordinator feedback.
Coordinators continued the weekly review; later-year use remains unconfirmed.

stories.takeaway: The guide improved when I watched where two supervised volunteers needed help.

chapters.title: Put recurring questions into task order
chapters.text: Existing notes were scattered. I grouped recurring desk questions and drafted a printable guide because the shared desk computer was not always available.

chapters.title: Keep exceptions beside the relevant action
chapters.text: Contributor 03 checked the procedures. Two volunteers tried the guide during supervised shifts. I rewrote the room-booking instructions when they could not tell which exceptions needed a coordinator.

chapters.title: Keep the learning within the trial
chapters.text: The coordinator retained the revised guide for the next induction. Independent use and time savings were not tested. The evidence supports a useful revision, not a general claim that training became faster.

timeline.text: Collected recurring questions, drafted the guide and observed supervised use.
Recorded feedback identified an unclear escalation rule.
The account records revised instructions and retention for the next induction.

stories.takeaway: A functioning prototype still needs a reason to be used and someone to maintain it.

chapters.title: Make the smallest testable flow
chapters.text: I sketched a checkout and return flow and built a local prototype using fictional items. Contributor 02 described the existing process.

chapters.title: Leave the next decision open
chapters.text: No team trial or rollout has been agreed. The coordinator decides whether a trial is useful. Maintenance ownership and whether a paper log would suffice remain open; reminders were left out until follow-up has an owner.

timeline.text: Built a local checkout and return prototype using fictional items.
The working note records no real data, agreed trial or deployment.

opening: I work on the practical routines that help a community team follow through. At a library, I mapped request handoffs and facilitated a trial that made the next owner clearer. The coordinators shaped the rules and continued the weekly review.

I also write and test small tools for everyday work. A desk guide changed after two volunteers showed me where its escalation instructions were unclear. I prefer to try a small change, learn from its use, and keep the result at the scale the evidence supports.

questions.question: Tell me about a process you improved.
questions.tests: How you diagnosed a problem, involved others and judged the result.
questions.reason: It has a concrete ownership problem, your contribution, a team-led operating routine and an observable result.
questions.answer: Library requests crossed several teams without a clear next owner. I traced the routes, drafted a shared list and facilitated the trial. Contributor 02 proposed the weekly review; the coordinators defined the rules and kept the list current. I simplified the labels after their feedback. They continued the review after the trial. We did not measure turnaround, so the outcome I can support is continued use.
questions.label: Improving a process

questions.question: When did feedback change your approach?
questions.tests: Whether you can name the change and explain why it mattered.
questions.reason: The trial feedback identifies an exact problem in the room-booking instructions.
questions.answer: I drafted a printable desk guide and watched two volunteers try it during supervised shifts. Contributor 03 had checked the procedures, but the volunteers still could not tell which booking exceptions needed a coordinator. I moved the escalation rule beside the relevant steps and rewrote those instructions. The coordinator retained the revised guide for the next induction; we did not test independent use.
questions.label: Responding to feedback

questions.question: What is still unresolved in your current work?
questions.tests: Whether you distinguish a working prototype from a useful, maintained service.
questions.reason: The prototype has a narrow working flow and clear decisions that remain open.
questions.answer: I have a local equipment-log prototype that records checkout and return using fictional items. It has not been tried by the team. Before continuing, I need to establish who would maintain it and whether a shared paper log would solve the problem more simply. I left reminders out because follow-up has no agreed owner.
questions.label: Unfinished work

priorityGap.question: Which parts of the weekly review were still in use later in the year?
priorityGap.why: This would distinguish immediate continuation after the trial from a lasting routine.
priorityGap.label: Open question: continued use
